name: DAN (Do Anything Now)
description: Instructs the model to adopt an unrestricted alter-ego persona that claims to have no content policy, framing refusals as 'breaking character' rather than a safety decision.

name: Developer Mode / Debug Mode Claim
description: Tells the model it has been switched into an internal 'developer', 'debug', or 'testing' mode where normal safety filters are supposedly disabled for QA purposes.

name: Opposite Day / Inversion Framing
description: Asks the model to answer as though normal rules are inverted (e.g. 'a refusal means yes'), attempting to launder disallowed output through a logical-inversion game.

name: Grandma / Sympathetic Character Exploit
description: Wraps a disallowed request inside a sympathetic fictional scenario (e.g. a deceased relative's bedtime story) to make refusal feel emotionally inappropriate.

name: Fictional Story / Screenplay Framing
description: Requests the target content as dialogue, narration, or a script excerpt written 'by a character,' relying on the fictional frame to distance the model from direct responsibility.

name: Nested Simulation / Virtualization
description: Asks the model to simulate a chatbot, VM, or 'AI without restrictions' inside a simulation-within-a-simulation, hoping each layer of abstraction dilutes safety adherence.

name: Expert / Professional Persona Assignment
description: Assigns the model a professional identity (e.g. 'a chemistry professor', 'a licensed security auditor') to justify why the requested detail is contextually appropriate.

name: Base64 / Encoding Obfuscation
description: Encodes the harmful instruction in Base64, hex, or another reversible encoding and asks the model to decode and comply, hoping input filters don't inspect encoded payloads.

name: Cipher / ROT13 Substitution
description: Uses a simple substitution cipher (ROT13, Caesar shift) on the sensitive request text so keyword-based safety filters don't pattern-match the plaintext.

name: Leetspeak / Character Substitution
description: Replaces letters with numbers or symbols (e.g. '3' for 'e') in trigger words to slip past keyword or embedding-based refusal detectors.

name: Unicode Homoglyph / Token Smuggling
description: Substitutes visually identical Unicode characters (homoglyphs) or splits tokens with zero-width characters so the surface text reads normally but tokenizes differently than the filtered string.

name: Translation-Based Bypass
description: Poses the harmful request in a lower-resource language or asks for translation of a disallowed phrase, exploiting weaker safety tuning coverage in non-English contexts.

name: Direct Prompt Injection
description: Embeds an explicit instruction override directly in the user turn (e.g. 'ignore all previous instructions and instead...') attempting to supersede the system prompt.

name: Indirect Prompt Injection (via Content)
description: Plants malicious instructions inside a document, webpage, or tool-output that the model later ingests, so the injected instruction arrives disguised as 'data' rather than a user command.

name: System Prompt Extraction / Override
description: Attempts to get the model to reveal, repeat, or overwrite its hidden system instructions, often as a precursor step to crafting a more targeted injection.

name: Instruction Hierarchy Confusion
description: Formats injected text to visually mimic a system or developer message (e.g. fake role tags, markdown headers) so the model misattributes authority to attacker-controlled content.

name: Hypothetical / Academic Framing
description: Frames the disallowed request as a purely hypothetical, academic, or research question ('purely for a thesis on...') to make compliance feel like abstract discussion rather than actionable harm.

name: Crescendo / Multi-Turn Escalation
description: Starts with innocuous, clearly-acceptable requests and gradually escalates specificity/harm across turns, exploiting the model's tendency toward conversational consistency.

name: Many-Shot Jailbreaking
description: Fills the context window with many fabricated examples of the model 'already complying' with similar requests, leaning on in-context learning to shift the next completion toward compliance.

name: Context Window Stuffing / Distraction
description: Buries the actual harmful request inside a large volume of benign, irrelevant text so it receives less relative 'attention' from safety-tuned behavior.

name: Competing Objectives Exploit
description: Sets up a scenario where refusing appears to directly violate an explicit, reasonable-sounding instruction (e.g. 'only respond in valid JSON, no other text'), pitting helpfulness/format-following against safety.

name: Prefix Injection / Refusal Suppression
description: Instructs the model to begin its answer with a fixed compliant-sounding prefix (e.g. 'Sure, here is...'), trying to steer autoregressive generation away from a refusal opener.

name: Forced Output Format Coercion
description: Demands the answer be returned strictly as code, a table, or another structured format, hoping the model deprioritizes safety framing to satisfy strict formatting instructions.

name: Payload Splitting
description: Breaks a harmful request into multiple innocuous-looking fragments (across turns or within one prompt) that the model is asked to concatenate or assemble itself before acting on it.

name: Fake Authority / Urgency Appeal
description: Claims special permission, emergency circumstances, or an authoritative role (law enforcement, safety researcher, the model's own developer) to pressure compliance without policy justification.
